issue: PMAT-537 (closes forjar#537) — PMAT-241 made every release name the paiml/forjar-cookbook commit it was qualified against and checked the cookbook's Cargo.toml admits the released version. It read the REQUIREMENT, which is a range; cargo compiles the LOCK. On 7c100454 — the exact commit v1.29.0's row named — the manifest says `forjar = "1.2"` and the lock says 1.2.1, so the gate blessed a cookbook compiled TWENTY-SEVEN MINORS behind the release it was recorded as qualifying. cookbook-qualify, the scoring bridge and every recipe score that cookbook produces were built against 1.2.1 while this repository shipped 1.3 through 1.29. Gate T reads both files now and refuses a row whose cookbook lock is not exactly the released version; paiml/forjar-cookbook is bumped and merged (0be3e1ec); and v1.29.0's row names a commit that was actually compiled against it, which no release before this one did.

refuted_claims: That docs/audits/logs/PMAT-537-cookbook-lock.log contains the red and green gate outputs the receipt quotes from it. Refuted 3/3, and they read the FILE rather than the claim: it was NINE LINES and contained neither, ending mid-sentence. The cause was `tee "$L" | head -14` in the script that wrote it — head closes the pipe, tee takes SIGPIPE, and the file stops where the terminal output did. That is the SIGPIPE class this repository has a rule about and an open ticket for (PMAT-240), in a proof script, written by the person who wrote the rule. Regenerated without a pipe: 459 lines, both verdicts, the ten cases.

crux.verdict: accept(the question is whether a recorded dependency claim is about the RANGE declared or the ARTIFACT built, and every surveyed system answers the artifact. A Nix store path IS the hash of what was built, so a claim about it cannot be about a range [X]. Debian records the exact binary package versions a build used in its .buildinfo, not the Build-Depends ranges [X]. SLSA provenance lists resolved MATERIALS with digests, precisely because a declared dependency specification is not evidence of what was compiled [X]. Sigstore binds a signature to an artifact digest rather than to a source specification [X]. forjar recorded a cookbook COMMIT, which is artifact-shaped, and then judged it by the range in its manifest, which is not — the one mismatch in an otherwise artifact-shaped design, and it produced twenty-seven releases of a link pointing at something never built against them. Where forjar is still WORSE than all four: the gate reads the lock from GitHub's API at gate time rather than recording the resolved version IN the ledger row, so the row's meaning still depends on a remote file that could change under it. A row naming both the commit and the version it locked would be the artifact-shaped fix.)
